content.title: Kitchen Fitting Costs in London 2027: 7 Things Your Quote Should Explain
content.summary: Seven fitting work packages, a responsibility sheet and the distinction between installed cabinets and a usable kitchen.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Fitting Costs London 2027: 7 Quote Checks | NURA
content.seo_description: Comparing kitchen fitting costs in London? Check 7 parts of your 2027 quote, including labour, plumbing, electrics, removal and separately priced work.

hero.alt: Clay kitchen cabinetry with an island, pale worktop and grouped cabinet and finish samples
hero.caption: Cabinet, panel and surface choices need a clearly defined fitting scope. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

social_image.alt: Clay kitchen cabinetry with an island, pale worktop and grouped cabinet and finish samples
social_image.caption: Cabinet, panel and surface choices need a clearly defined fitting scope. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Kitchen fitting costs in London are only comparable when the work behind each total is clear. For a 2027 project, ask for a current, site-specific quotation covering the seven areas below. Separate cabinet fitting from the work needed to make the room usable, and give every task a named responsibility. This is a scope guide, not a forecast of 2027 prices.
For context,
Checkatrade's kitchen fitting guide

, checked in October 2026, gives £2,000 to £6,000 for labour to fit a family kitchen, with £3,500 as its average. That is its UK benchmark for a described job, not a London average, a Nura price or a 2027 quotation. A price for cabinet installation alone and one covering several trades describe different commissions.
Use this guide when you have a layout and want to understand the fitting bill. For cabinet materials, hardware and the supplied specification, use the
bespoke kitchen quote comparison
. For the whole project budget, see
new kitchen costs in London
1. Removal, protection and access

Ask whether the price includes disconnecting the existing kitchen through the appropriate trades, removing units and worktops, carrying waste out and arranging disposal. Keep removal and disposal as separate questions: a stack of dismantled cabinets is not a cleared room.

Show the delivery and waste route, including stairs, lift restrictions and places where materials could be stored. Ask who prices parking, protection and any permissions needed for the proposed arrangements. Record which existing floors, doors or fittings must be retained. These details belong in the site assessment rather than an assumed London surcharge.
2. Cabinet assembly, fitting and visible panels

Attach the actual unit list and drawing revision. Ask whether assembly, positioning, fixing, door adjustment, handles, plinths, fillers and exposed ends are included. Identify any panels or trim supplied separately and who checks they have arrived before the relevant work starts.

An oak end panel beside painted doors is an aesthetic choice with installation consequences: the side, edge and junction with the wall need to be described, not left under a general heading of units. Agree what a finished cabinet run should look like. A fitting allowance cannot resolve an undecided panel detail.

body_nodes.alt: Clay tall cupboards with an oak end panel beside matching cabinet finish samples
body_nodes.caption: Visible ends and fillers deserve a place in the fitting scope alongside the cabinet list. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: 3. Plumbing and the usable sink

List the sink, tap, dishwasher and any other water-connected products by model. Ask which existing connections can be retained, what needs assessment and who prices alterations. Distinguish positioning an appliance from connecting it, checking it and leaving it usable.

If another contractor is doing the plumbing, name that responsibility on the same sheet. Ask what must be ready before the final connection visit and who arranges it. Do not assume that a fitted sink bowl means the kitchen has a working water supply and waste connection.
4. Electrics, gas and extraction

Give the relevant trades the appliance and lighting requirements, plus proposed positions. Ask for electrical alterations, final connections, extraction work and applicable testing or certification to be stated explicitly. The practical question is who assesses and prices each task, not whether a broad fitting label sounds comprehensive.
Gas work requires a Gas Safe registered engineer under
GOV.UK guidance
. Ask who is arranging that work where it applies. Do not treat moving a gas hob, changing an electrical appliance or choosing a new extractor as a cabinet-only decision. The
first-fix coordination guide
covers the wider sequence.
5. Worktops and separate visits

Record measurement or templating, fabrication, delivery, fitting, cut-outs and finishing as distinct tasks. Ask the chosen worktop supplier what must be ready before measurement and installation, and who confirms that readiness. The answer depends on the specified product and installation method.

Where the worktop and plumbing are separate commissions, identify who books the final connection after the surface is installed. Ask how a missed or additional visit would be priced. There is no useful universal return-visit allowance without the supplier's actual scope.
6. Walls, floors and decoration

Describe the intended finish beyond the cupboards: wall repairs, splashbacks, flooring edges, skirting and paint. Ask who assesses the substrate and who prices making good after removal or service alterations. Identify full-room work separately from local repairs.

If you want to retain a floor or splashback, show it in the brief and ask how the proposed work affects it. A new cabinet line can change what is visible. Agree how unresolved areas will be assessed before treating a repair allowance as a finished-room price.
7. Programme, changes and handover

Ask for the assumptions behind the programme, the person coordinating separate trades and the process for agreeing changes. Record the quotation's validity, payment stages, VAT presentation and any provisional amounts. Confirm how extra work and return visits are approved before they are commissioned.

Define handover in practical terms: the agreed work complete, identified defects recorded, applicable documents supplied and a contact for unresolved items. Separately ask when the sink and cooking appliances are expected to be usable. Cabinet fitting complete and kitchen usable may be different milestones; obtain the actual plan for your room.

body_nodes.alt: A pale kitchen worktop with a stainless steel sink, tap and open blank planning notebook
body_nodes.caption: Ask when the sink will be usable and which documents and checks belong at handover. Illustration, Nura Interiors.

children.text: Put the responsibilities on one sheet

For each row, add the written price reference, named contractor and status: included, separately quoted, allowance or unresolved. An unresolved task is not a zero-cost task. The examples below are questions to complete, not standard Nura contract inclusions.
Work package
Record before comparing totals
Removal and access
Who clears waste, protects retained finishes and prices access arrangements?
Cabinet fitting
Which units, panels, fillers and final adjustments are covered?
Plumbing
Who connects and checks each product, and what must be ready?
Electrics, gas and extraction
Who assesses, installs and supplies applicable documents?
Worktop visits
Who confirms readiness and arranges later connections?
Room finishes
Which repairs, flooring edges and decoration are included?
Programme and handover
Who coordinates, approves changes and resolves outstanding work?

The cabinet quote covers the panel, the surface supplier prices the worktop, and the plumbing responsibility is still unconfirmed. Their next step is to resolve the connection and readiness arrangements, rather than assuming the cabinet completion date answers both needs. No cost or completion date follows from this example.

content.title: Kitchen Table Centrepieces That Make Way for Dinner
content.summary: Set out an ordinary meal before deciding whether the centrepiece stays on the table or moves elsewhere.
content.seo_title: Kitchen Table Centrepieces for Everyday Meals | NURA

hero.alt: An oak kitchen table with four ivory place settings and a low empty ceramic vessel beside blue cabinetry

children.text: A kitchen table centrepiece should work with the meal, not just the empty table. Start with your usual place settings and serving dishes, then try one object you already own. Decide whether it can stay while you eat or needs a clear place elsewhere. Either answer can lead to a table you enjoy using.
Set the table before choosing the decoration

Begin without a centrepiece. Put out the plates, glasses and empty serving dishes you use for an ordinary meal, in their usual positions. Notice which part of the middle you actually use. A display for a table where food is served from the kitchen can be different from one where everyone shares dishes at the table.

Try a single stable, dry, empty vase in the remaining space. Keep the whole base supported and follow the care guidance for your table and the object. You are rehearsing your own arrangement, not following a universal rule about how much of the tabletop to fill.
Look from the chair as well as the doorway

Sit in the seats you normally use and compare the view across the table with the view from the kitchen entrance. Notice whether the object interrupts a view you want to keep, or makes reaching your place setting awkward.
